n: As the human family grows, the story turns toward a crisis. The book of Moses adds that Noah and his sons had daughters too, setting up the marriages described next.

The “sons of God” marry the “daughters of men” simply because they are attractive. Restoration scripture explains these were descendants of Noah who married outside the covenant into a wicked society, despite warnings.

f.g: Many interpretations exist. The book of Moses identifies covenant-keeping people, and notes that wicked men also falsely claimed the title.

n: God says His Spirit will not keep striving with people forever. A limit of 120 years is set—perhaps a final period for repentance before the Flood.

f.w: My spirit shall not always strive with man

f.g: Likely the time left before the Flood, though some read it as a new limit on human lifespan.

n: This era had “giants”—mighty, famous men. Fame and strength, however, came with violence and corruption, as the next verses show.

f.g: Hebrew nephilim — perhaps “fallen ones”; powerful, violent men. Compare Numbers 13:33.

n: God sees that human wickedness has become total: even people’s thoughts are constantly evil. Sin begins in the heart and imagination before it becomes action.

f.w: every imagination of the thoughts of his heart

n: God grieves deeply over humanity. He is not a distant force but a Father whose heart aches at His children’s choices. The JST says it was Noah who “repented” or grieved.

f.g: Hebrew naḥam — to be sorry or grieve. The JST/Moses 8:25 reads “it repented Noah, and his heart was pained.”

n: God announces that He will wipe out life on the earth. The destruction of creation mirrors the creation account in reverse—people, beasts, creeping things, and birds.
One man stands out. “Grace” here means God’s favor. Noah’s righteousness does not earn the Flood’s escape so much as respond to God’s gracious choice of him.
Noah’s story begins. He is just, whole-hearted, and like Enoch, “walked with God.” “Perfect” means complete or blameless, not flawless.

f.g: Hebrew tamim — whole, complete, blameless; spiritually mature.

n: Noah’s three sons are named again, as the family through whom humanity will continue.
The earth is corrupt and full of violence. In Hebrew, violence (ḥamas) means cruel injustice and bloodshed that ruins society.

f.g: Hebrew ḥamas — violent wrongdoing, cruelty, injustice.

n: God looks and sees that “all flesh” has ruined its way. The world He called “very good” has been spoiled by human choices.

f.g: Ruined, spoiled. The same Hebrew verb is translated “destroy” in verse 13—God brings an end to what people had already ruined.

n: God tells Noah that the end has come for this violent world. Moses 8 adds that Noah had preached repentance for years, but the people would not listen.

f.w: The end of all flesh is come before me

n: God gives Noah detailed instructions for a great boat with rooms, sealed inside and out with pitch. The same Hebrew word for “ark” is used for the basket that saved baby Moses.

f.g: Hebrew tevah — a box or chest; used elsewhere only for Moses’ basket (Exodus 2:3).
An unknown type of wood, perhaps cypress.

n: The ark is huge—about 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. Its proportions are those of a stable barge built to float, not to sail.

f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm), the length from elbow to fingertip.

n: The ark has an opening for light near the top, one door in the side, and three decks. Like the Jaredite barges, God guides the design for survival.

f.g: Hebrew tsohar — an opening for light, perhaps a roof gap running around the top.

n: God Himself will bring the Flood. The emphatic “I, even I” makes clear that this is God’s judgment, not random disaster.

f.g: Emphatic repetition stressing God’s direct action.

n: This is the first use of the word “covenant” in the Bible. God promises to preserve Noah and his family. Covenants become the backbone of God’s relationship with His people.

f.g: A binding, sacred agreement initiated by God.

n: Noah is to bring pairs of every kind of creature to keep life alive. The ark is a floating preservation of creation.
Birds, animals, and creeping things will “come unto” Noah—God will lead them to the ark.

f.g: The animals come to Noah; he does not have to hunt them down.

n: Noah must store food for his family and the animals. Faith includes practical preparation.

f.w: take thou unto thee of all food

n: Noah obeys completely. His faith is shown by building an ark for a flood no one could yet see.

f.w: according to all that God commanded him
